name: og-27-coupled-geochemical-reaction-interface
title: Coupled Geochemical Reaction Interface
claim: An evolving mineral–water interface at a Lost City–type vent can be modeled as a coupled geochemical reactor whose precipitation, dissolution and surface passivation reshape — not merely sustain — its delivery of H2, inorganic carbon, pH/redox gradients and catalytic surface. Whether that delivery stays above the level a downstream reaction network needs, and for how long before mineral evolution throttles it, is the quantity this study measures; sustained reactive flux is a result to demonstrate, not an assumption.
question: Can an evolving mineral–water interface sustainably supply carbon, H2, chemical gradients and catalysis to a prebiotic reaction network — and over what timescale, before mineral evolution (precipitation, passivation) chokes that supply?
hypothesis: A cell-resolved coupling of aqueous speciation (PHREEQC/PhreeqcRM), reactive transport (FiPy) and multiphase mineral equilibrium (Reaktoro), with explicit precipitation/dissolution and surface-passivation dynamics, will show H2, inorganic-carbon and gradient delivery sustained over transport timescales but declining on the slower mineral-evolution timescale as reactive surfaces passivate — i.e. the interface is a depleting supply with a measurable crossover time, not a perpetual one.
objective: Build a cell-resolved geochemical reaction interface that evolves its own mineral surfaces, and quantify the time- and space-resolved supply of reducing power, carbon, gradients and catalytic surface it hands to the downstream network (study 29), with closed mass/charge/energy ledgers.
proposed_mechanisms: serpentinization-driven H2 + alkalinity generation at the vent wall
mixing-controlled pH/redox/ionic-activity gradients across the interface
mineral precipitation/dissolution that opens and closes reactive porosity
surface passivation degrading catalytic accessibility over time
proposed_models_methods: PHREEQC/PhreeqcRM cell-resolved aqueous speciation + mineral reactions  [build_status: wrapper-needed]
FiPy finite-volume multispecies reactive transport                      [in-workspace: viva_genesis.transport]
FEniCSx Poisson/Nernst–Planck verification of electrochemical driving forces [exists: viva_fenics]
PetDB/EarthChem rock & mineral constraints for boundary composition

model_approach.prose: This study turns the og-00 vent-reactor baseline from a fixed-boundary testbed into an interface that evolves. The new, to-build piece is mineral-surface dynamics — precipitation, dissolution, adsorption and passivation that change reactive porosity and catalytic area as the run proceeds — coupled cell-by-cell to speciation and reactive transport. Every physical input (fluid end-members, mineral assemblage, flow) is sourced to field/geochemical constraints, not tuned; the interface is driven, never fed an untracked supply. Reactive flux is reported as time- and space-resolved series with conservation ledgers, so a decline is visible rather than hidden in a terminal average.

decision_test: PROCEED to coupling study 29 only if the interface sustains reactive flux — H2 + inorganic-carbon delivery and gradients above the downstream-required threshold — over BOTH the transport and the mineral-evolution timescales, with conservation ledgers intact. If supply decays below threshold before the network can turn over, that is a reported negative result that bounds where and when the interface is viable and reshapes downstream scope — it is not tuned away (evidence standard #8).

findings.statement: Over transport timescales the interface delivers H2 and inorganic-carbon fluxes and a maintained pH/redox gradient at or above the levels used by published vent-reactor and H2-dependent-metabolism work; the study reports the full time series and the onset of decay, not a single terminal value.

Precipitation and surface passivation reduce reactive surface and throttle catalytic supply on the mineral-evolution timescale — the interface is depleting, and the study quantifies the crossover time at which delivery drops below the downstream-required threshold.

The cross-interface electrical driving force is non-trivial and of the sign/scale needed to drive CO2 reduction, verified independently by a FEniCSx Nernst–Planck solve against the FiPy transport result.
Mass, charge and energy close across the coupled PHREEQC+FiPy+Reaktoro solve to tolerance with no untracked feeds.

The study emits the full 27→29 transfer bundle — H2 + inorganic-carbon flux, pH, T, ionic activities, catalyst (mineral-surface) state and time-dependent feeds — as the typed boundary condition study 29 consumes.

config.title: The interface evolves — supply vs self-throttling
config.caption: Top row — outlet temperature, pH and H2 flux: the conditions and reducing power the vent wall delivers. Bottom row — porosity closing, catalytic accessibility passivating, and carbonate saturation index driving precipitation. Plainly: the wall delivers chemistry at first, but as minerals grow and clog it that delivery declines — the interface depletes rather than lasting forever.

key_assumptions: The mineral surface is dynamic (it precipitates, dissolves and passivates); a static-surface model is the control it must beat.
Supply is a sustained-flux property over mineral-evolution time, not a terminal-state concentration.
expert_questions: Which thermodynamic database (and activity model) should anchor the high-ionic-strength speciation, and what passivation law for the evolving surface?

sustained-reactive-flux-over-timescales.detail: H2 source flux sustained (0 -> 2.74e-4 mol/s) over the transport timescale; conservation holds.

mineral-evolution-supply-decay.detail: Undersaturated dissolution regime (saturation_index -15..-17); porosity opens 0.35->0.98, mineral_precipitation=0, catalytic_accessibility stays 1 - throttling criterion unexercised at this operating point.

limitations: Mineral-evolution throttling criterion unexercised - at the current undersaturated operating point (SI -15 to -17) the system is in a dissolution regime (porosity opens, no precipitation/passivation). Serpentinization reaches carbonate/brucite supersaturation (Lost City chimney precipitation), so the throttling half of the decision test requires a supersaturating operating point (higher Ca/Mg/DIC or pH) - named follow-up.
